deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files from a USB Flash Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on a USB flash drive can often be recovered with PhotoRec if you stop using it. Safe step-by-step guide for beginners.
deleted.summary: When you delete a file from a USB drive, the drive usually just forgets where the file was. The data itself stays until new files overwrite it. Most flash drives do not use TRIM (a feature that tells a drive to wipe deleted space), so recovery chances are often good if you act quickly. Every new file you save lowers the odds.
deleted.riskNote: Scanning from a copy is safe, but saving anything new to the drive can overwrite the deleted files for good.
stopFirst: Stop saving or copying anything to the USB drive. New files can overwrite the deleted ones.
Do not install recovery software onto the USB drive for the same reason.
Do not format the drive, even if Windows asks you to. Formatting makes recovery harder.

steps.title: Unplug and stop
steps.detail: Every new file you save can overwrite a deleted one. Unplugging keeps the deleted files where they are.
how: Windows: click the small arrow in the taskbar near the clock, click the USB icon and choose Eject. Mac: drag the drive icon to the Trash (it turns into an Eject button) or right-click it > Eject.
Wait for the message that it is safe to remove, then pull it out.
Put it somewhere safe and do not use it again until recovery is done.

steps.title: Check the Recycle Bin and backups
steps.detail: Free and risk-free. Files deleted from a USB drive often skip the bin, but a copy may exist elsewhere.
how: Windows: open the Recycle Bin on the desktop, look for your file, right-click it and choose Restore.
Mac: click the Trash in the Dock, right-click the file and choose Put Back.
Check cloud services (OneDrive, iCloud, Google Drive) and email attachments for copies.
Check your phone, other computers and old backup drives.

steps.title: Make an image of the USB drive
steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole USB drive saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. Doing this first protects you if the drive starts failing. Type the USB drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases the USB drive.
how: You need a second drive with free space at least as big as the USB drive. Plug it in and note its name.

Windows: ddrescue runs from Linux, so follow the Live USB guide to start your PC from a Linux USB stick (a stick that starts a temporary Linux without touching your drive). When the Linux desktop appears, press Ctrl+Alt+T to open the Terminal and type `sudo apt install gddrescue` (the imaging guide explains what to do if it is not found). Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter, then type `brew install ddrescue` (needs Homebrew from brew.sh).

Find the USB drive's name. Linux: type `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL` and match it by size (it looks like sdb, which you type as /dev/sdb). Mac: type `diskutil list` (it looks like /dev/disk4). Pick by size, never guess. Then open the destination drive in the Files app (Mac: Finder) so it is ready, but do not open the USB drive.
Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.map`. Replace sdX with the USB drive's name and DEST with your destination drive's name (on Linux Mint the folder is /media/mint/ instead). On a Mac, use /dev/diskN as the first path and /Volumes/DEST/ for the other two. The first path is the USB drive (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the USB drive.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the .map file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Try TestDisk first
steps.detail: TestDisk can often bring back deleted files with their original names and folders. It is the quickest option.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: download it from cgsecurity.org, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then right-click `testdisk_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator. Linux live USB: in the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) type `sudo apt install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`. Mac: in Terminal type `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`.
If you made an image, start TestDisk on the image instead: type `sudo testdisk /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` (use your own folder and file name). Otherwise it lists your drives.
Choose `Create` (log file), pick the drive or image with the arrow keys, choose `Proceed`, then accept the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose your partition, press `Advanced`, then `Undelete`. Deleted files show in red. Press `c` to copy a file, then pick a folder on a different drive.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec next
steps.detail: If TestDisk cannot find your files, PhotoRec searches the drive's contents directly. It works even when the file list is gone, but names are lost.
how: Open PhotoRec (a free tool that searches for file contents instead of file names; it comes with TestDisk). Windows: in the unzipped TestDisk folder, right-click `qphotorec_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator (this version has buttons). Linux live USB: type `sudo apt install testdisk` if you have not yet, then `sudo photorec /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` to search your image. Mac: `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo photorec`. The text version uses the arrow keys and Enter.

Pick the drive or image from the list (text version: then choose `Proceed`), then the partition, or the `Whole disk` line if unsure. When asked for the file system, pick `Other` (the window version calls it FAT/NTFS/HFS+/ReiserFS/...) unless it was a Linux drive (`ext2/ext3/ext4`). Choose `Free` for deleted files, or `Whole` for formatted, RAW or damaged drives.

Click `File Formats` and untick types you do not need to save time. Some names differ from the file endings: keep `jpg` and `png` for photos, `mov` for MP4 and MOV videos, `pdf`, and `zip` for DOCX and XLSX. Text version: choose `File Opt` before `Search`, press `s` to untick everything, tick types with the Space bar, then press `q` to go back. Skipping this is also fine.

Choose where to save results: a folder on a different drive, never the USB drive itself. Window version: click `Browse`. Text version: after `Search` it shows a list of folders; move to /media/ubuntu/DEST with the arrow keys and Enter, then press `C`.
Window version: click `Search`. It can take hours. Leave the computer on until it says it has finished.

steps.title: Save to a different drive
steps.detail: Saving recovered files back onto the USB drive would overwrite files you have not recovered yet.
how: When the tool asks where to save, choose a folder on your computer's main drive or another external drive.
Make sure it has at least as much free space as the USB drive.
Never pick the USB drive or its image file as the destination.
Check the free space first. Windows: open This PC. Mac: right-click the drive > Get Info.

steps.title: Sort and check
steps.detail: PhotoRec names files with numbers, so you have to look at them yourself.
how: Open the folder PhotoRec or TestDisk saved into. PhotoRec makes folders called `recup_dir.1`, `recup_dir.2` and so on with numbered file names.
Windows: click Sort by > Type in File Explorer. Mac: click View > as List, then click the Kind column.
Double-click a few files of each type. A photo that shows, a document that opens or a video that plays means it worked.
Files that will not open, or look blank or all gray, are damaged or already erased. Open a few more before deciding.

deleted.callPro: If the drive disconnects while copying, or critical files do not turn up, ask a professional.

faq.q: Why can I recover deleted files from a flash drive?
faq.a: Deleting usually just removes the file's entry from the list. The data stays on the drive until something new is written over it.

faq.q: Do deleted USB files go to the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: On Windows, usually not: they are removed right away. A Mac may keep them in the Trash until you empty it, so check there.

formatted.title: Recover Files from a Formatted USB Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Formatted a USB flash drive by mistake? A quick format often leaves data recoverable. Learn the safe order: image first, then TestDisk or PhotoRec.
formatted.summary: A quick format only wipes the file list (the index of what is stored where), so much of the data is usually still on the USB drive. A full format on Windows Vista and later writes zeros over the whole drive, and that data is gone for good. Recovery works best if you have not copied anything new onto it.
formatted.riskNote: The scans are safe when run on a copy, but saving new files or formatting again reduces what can come back.
stopFirst: Do not copy new files onto the drive. They overwrite old ones.
Do not format it again or change its file system (the way it is organized).
Do not install recovery software onto the USB drive.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If you did a quick format, the old data is probably still there. Anything you write now could replace it.
how: Windows: click the small arrow near the clock, click the USB icon and choose Eject. Mac: right-click the drive icon > Eject.
Do not open, rename or save anything on it.
If you remember choosing 'Quick Format' (Windows) or 'Erase' (Mac), the odds are better. Note that for later.

steps.title: Review and organize
steps.detail: Opening samples tells you whether the drive was quick-formatted or fully wiped.
how: Open the recovered folder. PhotoRec makes `recup_dir.1`, `recup_dir.2` and so on.
Windows: click Sort by > Type. Mac: View > as List.
Open a few files of each type.
If most are broken or blank, the drive was probably fully formatted or heavily reused.

not-detected.title: USB Flash Drive Not Detected or Not Showing
not-detected.metaDescription: USB drive not showing up? Try simple checks first, image it if it appears, and learn when a broken connector or dead controller needs a pro.
not-detected.summary: A USB drive may not appear because of a bad port, a missing drive letter, damaged files, a worn connector or a failed controller (the small chip that runs the drive). Many cases are simple to check. Real hardware failure is harder and often needs a specialist.
not-detected.riskNote: Basic checks are safe, but forcing a damaged connector or soldering without experience can break the drive for good.
stopFirst: Do not click Format if Windows offers it. That wipes the file list.
Do not keep bending or wiggling the plug.
Do not use heat, glue or a soldering iron on it.

steps.title: Try another port and computer
steps.detail: A bad port or driver is a common cause, and this check is harmless.
how: Unplug the drive and plug it into a different USB port, ideally on the back of a desktop.
Do not use a USB hub or extension cable for this test.
Try a different computer.
If a window offers to format or scan, click Cancel.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: These built-in tools list every drive, even ones with no drive letter or an unknown format (shown as RAW, meaning the computer cannot read how it is organized).
how: Windows: right-click the Start button and choose Disk Management. If a window pops up asking to initialize the disk, click Cancel. Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Disk Utility and press Enter, then click View > Show All Devices.
Look for a drive of the right size. A drive with no letter, or labelled RAW or Unallocated, may still hold your files.
Do not click Initialize, Format or Delete Volume. Just write down what you see.
If nothing of the right size appears, go to the next step.

steps.title: Inspect the connector
steps.detail: A bent, loose or cracked plug is a hardware fault. Software cannot fix it.
how: Unplug the drive and hold it in good light.
Look at the metal plug for bends, cracks or a wobble where it joins the case.
Gently check if the plug moves. If it does, stop.
Leave any soldering repair to a repair shop or lab.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: The copy may hold a damaged partition (a section of the drive). TestDisk can find it, and PhotoRec can pull out files if it cannot.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). steps.title: Know the limits
steps.detail: If the drive never appears, or shows 0 MB or an unknown device, the controller or memory chip is likely failing. A lab can sometimes read the memory chip directly.
how: Decide how valuable the files are. If they cannot be replaced, stop experimenting.
Search for data recovery labs near you. Look for a free evaluation and a 'no data, no fee' promise.
Describe your exact problem and ask for a price range before you send anything.
Pack the device in an anti-static bag or bubble wrap and ship it only after you agree on terms.

not-detected.callPro: If it is not detected on any computer, or the plug is broken, ask a professional.

faq.q: Why does my USB drive show 0 bytes?
faq.a: The controller often cannot read the memory chip properly. This is usually a hardware fault that software cannot fix.

faq.q: Can a broken USB plug be fixed?
faq.a: Sometimes, by soldering on a new connector, but it takes skill and a slip can destroy the data. Leave it to a repair shop or lab.

no-power.title: USB Flash Drive Dead or No Light
no-power.metaDescription: USB drive with no light or no response? Rule out ports and cables, then learn when a failed controller means chip-off recovery by a professional.
no-power.summary: A USB drive that does nothing, with no light, may have a broken connector, a short circuit or a failed controller (the chip that runs it). First rule out the port and computer. If it is dead everywhere, it may need hardware-level work.
no-power.riskNote: A drive that is hot or shorted can be damaged more by repeated plugging, and DIY soldering is easy to get wrong.
stopFirst: Do not keep plugging it in if it gets hot or smells burnt.
Do not keep plugging it in and out hoping it wakes up.
Do not open the case or touch the chips with a soldering iron.

steps.title: Test the port
steps.detail: The problem may be the port or computer, not the drive.
how: Plug in a USB device that works, such as a mouse, to the same port.
If that device works, the port is fine. If not, try other ports.
Then plug the drive into other ports and a second computer.
Do this once per port, not repeatedly.

steps.title: Check for a light or warmth
steps.detail: A light shows power is reaching the drive. Heat means a possible short circuit.
how: Plug the drive in and look for an LED (small light) on it.
Touch it gently with a finger after a few seconds. If it feels hot, unplug it at once.
Note whether it lights up, stays dark or gets warm.
If it is hot, do not plug it in again.

steps.title: Inspect the plug
steps.detail: Dirt, bends and cracks stop the contacts from touching.
how: Unplug the drive and look at the metal plug in good light.
Look for bent metal, cracks, loose parts and dust.
Brush dust away with a dry soft brush. Do not use liquid.
If the plug is cracked or loose, stop.

steps.detail: The copy lets you search for lost files without touching the damaged drive again.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). steps.title: Consider a professional
steps.detail: If it stays dead, a lab can sometimes read the memory chip directly, but results vary. Many small drives are monolith designs (chip and controller sealed in one piece), which need special tools.
how: Decide how valuable the files are. If they cannot be replaced, stop experimenting.
Search for data recovery labs near you. Look for a free evaluation and a 'no data, no fee' promise.
Describe your exact problem and ask for a price range before you send anything.
Pack the device in an anti-static bag or bubble wrap and ship it only after you agree on terms.

faq.q: Is a dead USB drive always lost?
faq.a: No. If the memory chip is fine, a specialist can sometimes read it directly, though that costs time and money.

faq.q: Can I fix a broken USB connector myself?
faq.a: It is possible with soldering skills, but a mistake can destroy the data. Leave it to a repair shop or lab for anything important.

liquid-fire.title: USB Flash Drive Damaged by Water or Heat
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Washed or burned a USB flash drive? Do not plug it in or heat-dry it. Learn the safest way to handle it and when to call a professional.
liquid-fire.summary: USB flash drives are fairly tough, and some survive a wash. Liquid, heat or fire can still corrode the board or short the chip. Plugging it in before it is clean and dry can cause a short that ruins it.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Powering on a wet or dirty drive can short it, and heating it can damage the memory chip.
stopFirst: Do not plug it in while it is wet or dirty.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven, microwave or rice.
Do not scrub the contacts or open the case.

steps.title: Keep it unplugged
steps.detail: Power on a wet drive is what causes damage. Looking fine is not proof it is safe.
how: Leave the drive out of every computer, charger and USB port.
Pick it up by the sides, not the metal plug.
Lay it on a clean towel.

steps.title: Do not rinse or clean it
steps.detail: Cleaning leftovers off safely needs lab tools. Rinsing can push dirt and salt deeper in.
how: If it got salt water, mud, soda or another sugary drink on it, leave it exactly as it is.
Do not rinse, wipe, scrub or brush it.
Put it in a clean, dry bag or box.
Go straight to the professional step.

steps.title: Air dry only after clean water
steps.detail: Clean fresh water leaves nothing behind, so letting it dry by itself is safe. Heat is not, and anything other than clean water needs a lab.
how: Use this step only if the drive got clean fresh water, for example in the washing machine.
Stand it plug-end down on a clean towel at room temperature.
Leave it for several days. Do not use a hair dryer, oven, microwave or rice.
After salt water, sugary drinks, mud or fire, skip this and go to a professional.

steps.title: Inspect before using
steps.detail: Corrosion and burns tell you not to plug it in.
how: Look at the metal plug and body in good light.
Look for rust, green or white residue, cracks and burn marks.
If you see any of these, do not plug it in.
If it looks clean and dry after several days, go on to the copy.

steps.title: Make an image of the USB drive
steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole USB drive saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. If it looks clean and dry and shows up, copy it right away. Type the USB drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases the USB drive.
how: You need a second drive with free space at least as big as the USB drive. Plug it in and note its name.

Windows: ddrescue runs from Linux, so follow the Live USB guide to start your PC from a Linux USB stick (a stick that starts a temporary Linux without touching your drive). When the Linux desktop appears, press Ctrl+Alt+T to open the Terminal and type `sudo apt install gddrescue` (the imaging guide explains what to do if it is not found). Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter, then type `brew install ddrescue` (needs Homebrew from brew.sh).

Find the USB drive's name. Linux: type `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL` and match it by size (it looks like sdb, which you type as /dev/sdb). Mac: type `diskutil list` (it looks like /dev/disk4). Pick by size, never guess. Then open the destination drive in the Files app (Mac: Finder) so it is ready, but do not open the USB drive.
Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.map`. Replace sdX with the USB drive's name and DEST with your destination drive's name (on Linux Mint the folder is /media/mint/ instead). On a Mac, use /dev/diskN as the first path and /Volumes/DEST/ for the other two. The first path is the USB drive (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the USB drive.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the .map file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: TestDisk and PhotoRec search the copy for your files, so the fragile drive is not used again.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: download it from cgsecurity.org, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then right-click `testdisk_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator. Linux live USB: in the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) type `sudo apt install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`. Mac: in Terminal type `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`.
If you made an image, start TestDisk on the image instead: type `sudo testdisk /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` (use your own folder and file name). Otherwise it lists your drives.
Choose `Create` (log file), pick the drive or image with the arrow keys, choose `Proceed`, then accept the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose `Analyse`, then `Quick Search`, and copy found files to another drive. If nothing shows, run PhotoRec on the image.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it.

steps.title: Get professional help
steps.detail: Burns, corrosion or a drive that will not appear after drying call for a lab. Labs have tools to clean the board and read the chip safely.
how: Decide how valuable the files are. If they cannot be replaced, stop experimenting.
Search for data recovery labs near you. Look for a free evaluation and a 'no data, no fee' promise.
Describe your exact problem and ask for a price range before you send anything.
Pack the device in an anti-static bag or bubble wrap and ship it only after you agree on terms.

liquid-fire.callPro: If it is burned, cracked, corroded or not detected after drying, stop and call a professional.

faq.q: Can a USB drive survive the washing machine?
faq.a: Often yes, if it is fully dried before use. Waiting several days is safer than plugging it in right away.

faq.q: Is heat drying safe for a flash drive?
faq.a: No. Heat can damage the memory chip and the solder joints.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted USB Flash Drive Without Data Loss
corrupted.metaDescription: USB drive says RAW, asks to format, or files will not open? Image it first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec. Do not format or run chkdsk yet.
corrupted.summary: A corrupted USB drive has damaged file system information (the index of what is stored where). It often shows as RAW, meaning the computer cannot read how it is organized, usually after being pulled out too early or from worn memory. The files are often still there. Making a copy before any repair keeps your options open.
corrupted.riskNote: Formatting or running chkdsk can overwrite the information you need, and a failing drive may get worse with each use.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when Windows asks you to. That wipes the index you need.
Do not run chkdsk or any 'repair' prompt before making an image.
Do not install recovery software onto the USB drive.

steps.title: Stop and unplug
steps.detail: Prompts that offer to repair or format change the drive. Declining them keeps your files safe.
how: If a window says you need to format the disk, click Cancel.
Windows: eject from the arrow near the clock. Mac: right-click the drive > Eject.
Do not click Check Disk, Scan and Fix, or First Aid yet.

steps.title: Make an image of the USB drive
steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole USB drive saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. This also shows which areas are unreadable. Type the USB drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases the USB drive.
how: You need a second drive with free space at least as big as the USB drive. Plug it in and note its name.

Windows: ddrescue runs from Linux, so follow the Live USB guide to start your PC from a Linux USB stick (a stick that starts a temporary Linux without touching your drive). When the Linux desktop appears, press Ctrl+Alt+T to open the Terminal and type `sudo apt install gddrescue` (the imaging guide explains what to do if it is not found). Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter, then type `brew install ddrescue` (needs Homebrew from brew.sh).

Find the USB drive's name. Linux: type `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL` and match it by size (it looks like sdb, which you type as /dev/sdb). Mac: type `diskutil list` (it looks like /dev/disk4). Pick by size, never guess. Then open the destination drive in the Files app (Mac: Finder) so it is ready, but do not open the USB drive.
Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.map`. Replace sdX with the USB drive's name and DEST with your destination drive's name (on Linux Mint the folder is /media/mint/ instead). On a Mac, use /dev/diskN as the first path and /Volumes/DEST/ for the other two. The first path is the USB drive (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the USB drive.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the .map file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Try TestDisk on the image
steps.detail: A partition is a section of the drive. TestDisk can find a lost one or repair a damaged boot sector (the part that says how the drive starts).
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: download it from cgsecurity.org, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then right-click `testdisk_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator. Linux live USB: in the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) type `sudo apt install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`. Mac: in Terminal type `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`.
If you made an image, start TestDisk on the image instead: type `sudo testdisk /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` (use your own folder and file name). Otherwise it lists your drives.
Choose `Create` (log file), pick the drive or image with the arrow keys, choose `Proceed`, then accept the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Choose `Analyse`, then `Quick Search`. If your folders appear, press `p` to browse and `c` to copy files to a different drive. Do not choose `Write`.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if folders are lost
steps.detail: PhotoRec recovers files by type from the image. Names and folders are not kept.
how: Open PhotoRec (a free tool that searches for file contents instead of file names; it comes with TestDisk). Windows: in the unzipped TestDisk folder, right-click `qphotorec_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator (this version has buttons). Linux live USB: type `sudo apt install testdisk` if you have not yet, then `sudo photorec /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` to search your image. Mac: `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo photorec`. The text version uses the arrow keys and Enter.

Pick the drive or image from the list (text version: then choose `Proceed`), then the partition, or the `Whole disk` line if unsure. When asked for the file system, pick `Other` (the window version calls it FAT/NTFS/HFS+/ReiserFS/...) unless it was a Linux drive (`ext2/ext3/ext4`). Choose `Free` for deleted files, or `Whole` for formatted, RAW or damaged drives.

Click `File Formats` and untick types you do not need to save time. Some names differ from the file endings: keep `jpg` and `png` for photos, `mov` for MP4 and MOV videos, `pdf`, and `zip` for DOCX and XLSX. Text version: choose `File Opt` before `Search`, press `s` to untick everything, tick types with the Space bar, then press `q` to go back. Skipping this is also fine.

Choose where to save results: a folder on a different drive, never the USB drive itself. Window version: click `Browse`. Text version: after `Search` it shows a list of folders; move to /media/ubuntu/DEST with the arrow keys and Enter, then press `C`.
Window version: click `Search`. It can take hours. Leave the computer on until it says it has finished.

steps.title: Save to a different drive
steps.detail: Saving back onto the USB drive would overwrite your files.
how: Choose a folder on your computer or another external drive.
Make sure there is enough free space.
Open a few files to make sure they work.

steps.title: Fix the USB last
steps.detail: Only after your files are safe is it fine to wipe the drive. Flash memory wears out, so a drive that keeps corrupting should be replaced.
how: Windows: right-click the drive in File Explorer > Format > Start. Mac: Disk Utility > select the drive > Erase.
This erases everything, so check your recovered files first.
If the drive keeps corrupting later, buy a new one and stop using this one.

corrupted.callPro: If copying keeps failing, the drive disconnects or it shows the wrong size, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Why does my USB say I need to format the disk?
faq.a: The file system information is damaged. Your files may still be present, so do not format until you have a copy.

faq.q: Is it safe to run chkdsk on a corrupted USB drive?
faq.a: Not before you have a copy. Chkdsk changes the drive and can delete data it cannot fix.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted USB Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked USB drive from BitLocker To Go, VeraCrypt or a hardware PIN? Without the key recovery is not realistic. Learn where keys are often saved.
encrypted.summary: Encrypted USB drives scramble data so it cannot be read without the password or recovery key (a long code saved when encryption was turned on). If you have neither, recovery is not realistic. Many people can find the key in a Microsoft account or a password manager.
encrypted.riskNote: Wrong resets or an erase on a hardware-encrypted stick can destroy the key and make the data permanently unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not reset the drive or keep guessing its PIN. Many keypad drives wipe themselves after a set number of wrong tries.
Do not format it to get access. That erases the data.
Do not use tools that claim to crack or guess encryption.

steps.title: Identify the type
steps.detail: How it was locked decides where the key is.
how: Plug the drive in. Windows: a padlock on the drive icon in File Explorer means BitLocker To Go.
A drive with a keypad on its case uses hardware encryption.
A drive holding a program or file called VeraCrypt uses VeraCrypt.
Check the drive's label or box for a vendor name and look up its manual.

steps.title: Find the key
steps.detail: BitLocker recovery keys are usually saved online or printed.
how: BitLocker: go to aka.ms/myrecoverykey (it opens account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey) on any device and sign in with your Microsoft account. Also check any work or school account.
Look for a printout, or a text file on another drive or in email.
A BitLocker key is 48 digits in 8 groups.
Match the key ID on the lock screen to the one shown online.

steps.title: Search your passwords
steps.detail: The password is often in a manager, notes or an email.
how: Search your password manager for the drive name, BitLocker or VeraCrypt.
Search email and notes for 'recovery key'.
Check old documents and sticky notes.

steps.title: Unlock normally
steps.detail: Once you have the key, unlocking is the safe way in.
how: Plug the drive into a working computer.
Windows (BitLocker): double-click the drive, click More options > Enter recovery key, type it and click Unlock.
VeraCrypt: open the VeraCrypt app, click Select Device, pick the drive, click Mount and enter the password.
Copy the files to another drive.

steps.title: Make an image of the USB drive
steps.detail: An image is an exact copy of the whole USB drive saved as one file. You then run every recovery tool on the copy, so the original is never touched again. ddrescue is the free tool that makes the copy and keeps going past unreadable spots. Only do this if you have the key and the drive is damaged. It works for BitLocker or VeraCrypt, not keypad drives, and you unlock the copy afterwards. Type the USB drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases the USB drive.
how: You need a second drive with free space at least as big as the USB drive. Plug it in and note its name.

Windows: ddrescue runs from Linux, so follow the Live USB guide to start your PC from a Linux USB stick (a stick that starts a temporary Linux without touching your drive). When the Linux desktop appears, press Ctrl+Alt+T to open the Terminal and type `sudo apt install gddrescue` (the imaging guide explains what to do if it is not found). Mac: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter, then type `brew install ddrescue` (needs Homebrew from brew.sh).

Find the USB drive's name. Linux: type `lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL` and match it by size (it looks like sdb, which you type as /dev/sdb). Mac: type `diskutil list` (it looks like /dev/disk4). Pick by size, never guess. Then open the destination drive in the Files app (Mac: Finder) so it is ready, but do not open the USB drive.
Mac only: type `diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4` (use your number) so the Mac lets go of it. Do not click Initialize or Erase if a window pops up.

Type `sudo ddrescue -n /dev/sdX /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.map`. Replace sdX with the USB drive's name and DEST with your destination drive's name (on Linux Mint the folder is /media/mint/ instead). On a Mac, use /dev/diskN as the first path and /Volumes/DEST/ for the other two. The first path is the USB drive (the source), the second is where the copy goes. Swapping them erases the USB drive.
Wait until it says it is finished. Keep the .map file: it lets you stop and resume. Work only on an image file from now on.

steps.title: Run recovery after unlocking
steps.detail: If files are missing, TestDisk and PhotoRec can search the unlocked volume or its image.
how: Open TestDisk (a free tool that finds lost partitions, meaning the sections of a drive, and deleted files). Windows: download it from cgsecurity.org, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then right-click `testdisk_win.exe` and choose Run as administrator. Linux live USB: in the Terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T) type `sudo apt install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`. Mac: in Terminal type `brew install testdisk`, then `sudo testdisk`.
If you made an image, start TestDisk on the image instead: type `sudo testdisk /media/ubuntu/DEST/usb.img` (use your own folder and file name). Otherwise it lists your drives.
Choose `Create` (log file), pick the drive or image with the arrow keys, choose `Proceed`, then accept the partition table type it suggests, usually `Intel/PC` or `EFI GPT`, and press Enter.
Point TestDisk or PhotoRec at the unlocked drive or image, choose `Analyse` and `Quick Search`, and copy files to another drive.
Use the arrow keys and Enter to move around and `q` to go back. TestDisk only changes anything if you choose Write, so do not choose it.

encrypted.callPro: If the drive is encrypted and failing, or its hardware controller has died, ask a professional and expect it may not be possible.

faq.q: Can I recover files from a locked USB without the password?
faq.a: Realistically no. Good encryption cannot be bypassed, and anyone who promises otherwise should be treated with caution.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker key stored?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, in a work or school account, on a printout or in a file you saved earlier.
